report.source_text: A pterional craniotomy was performed on the right side under general anaesthesia with the patient in a supine position. After reaching the base of the brain and evacuation of fluid from basal cisterns, the tumour’s wall was cut, and a thick yellowish fluid was drained. The tumour was separated from the right optic nerve, right ICA, optic chiasm and left optic nerve. Instead of the pituitary stalk, two thin bands were found, extending from the third ventricle and running towards the sella turcica on both sides of the tumour. After separating the tumour from those bands, it was incised slightly above the sellar diaphragm, dissected from the third ventricle wall, along the lamina terminalis, and removed. After achieving haemostasis, the dura mater was sutured and fixed to the bone and a cranioplasty was performed. A suction drain was then placed, soft tissues were closed in layers and protected with a dressing.

report.source_text: Increasing intracranial pressure required the placement of external drainage on day 11 after tumour resection. On day 14 post-surgery, the external drainage was removed following a CT scan of the head which showed the ventricular system without features of hydrocephalus. After removal of the drain, the patient was in good general status and was verbally responsive. Neurological examination showed the presence of meningeal symptoms and slight strabismus in the left eye, decreased muscle tone and diminished asymmetrical tendineae reflexes in the upper extremities, with a predominance of the left side, and a decrease in muscle tone with areflexia and a positive Babinski sign on the right side in the lower extremities.

report.source_text: Six months after the procedure she still needed substitutional hormone therapy, anti-epileptic treatment and ophthalmic and psychological counselling. A systematic improvement in the patient’s condition was noticeable. Currently, the patient is in good neurological condition without focal damage to the central nervous system. clinician.trajectory_summary: A 7-year-old girl with no prior medical history presented with acute severe headache, vomiting, muscle weakness, and balance disorders, with concentration problems noted 2-3 months prior. Preoperative CT imaging revealed a large cystic tumor with peripheral calcifications in the sella/suprasellar region causing acute hydrocephalus. Pathological examination confirmed craniopharyngioma WHO G1. Right pterional craniotomy was performed with gross total resection, during which thick yellowish fluid was drained from the tumor cyst. Postoperative day 7 cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis demonstrated aseptic meningitis: pleocytosis (18 cells/μl with 60% neutrophils and 38% lymphocytes), elevated protein (154 mg/dl), normal glucose (79 mg%), elevated lactic acid (2.7 mmol/l), positive Pandy's reaction, and negative Nonne-Apelt reaction. Bacterial cultures (aerobic and anaerobic) and latex test were negative. Viral serology was negative for CMV, EBV, HSV, poxvirus, and Borrelia burgdorferi IgM antibodies. Blood and urine cultures were also negative. External ventricular drainage was placed on postoperative day 11 for increased intracranial pressure and removed on day 14 after CT showed resolution of hydrocephalus. The patient demonstrated systematic improvement over the postoperative course and at 6 months follow-up was in good neurological condition without focal central nervous system damage, though requiring hormone substitution, anti-epileptic treatment, and supportive counseling.
